strengths: The paper explores a promising alternative to rendered 2D pose conditioning: discrete tokens derived from SMPL joint sequences and injected into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through dedicated motion attention.
The proposed system is reasonably well described, with useful architecture, optimization, compute, sampling, dataset-curation, failure-case, and codebook details in the appendix.
Reported results are strong on several TikTok metrics: the method obtains the best FVD, FID-VID, LPIPS, and FID in the presented comparison, including a particularly large FID-VID improvement.

Ablations cover quantization, several positional-encoding variants, and classifier-free guidance strength. The qualitative examples span realistic and stylized references and identify limitations involving unusual anatomy and hand articulation.
The paper acknowledges misuse, consent, copyright, and identity-manipulation risks, although the proposed safeguards remain prospective.
weaknesses: The central claim that raw 3D motion tokens are better than rendered 2D pose guidance is not established by a controlled experiment. There is no same-backbone comparison against skeleton, mesh, depth, continuous-joint, or projected-SMPL conditioning. Comparisons instead conflate representation choice with a roughly 7B-parameter CogVideoX-based model, proprietary training data, architecture, and compute.

Quantitative evaluation is confined to TikTok sequences 335–340, apparently only six test videos. No uncertainty, repeated runs, or statistical analysis is reported. FID/FVD estimates on such a small set are questionable, and the broad open-world claims receive only selected qualitative support—without pose-accuracy, temporal-consistency, or identity metrics and without a human study.

The paper overstates its table by claiming superiority across all metrics: MTVCrafter is worse than multiple baselines on PSNR and SSIM. Baseline comparability is also unclear because some numbers are copied from original papers while others are produced under the authors' evaluation setting, with no controlled matching of resolution, training data, model size, or pose estimator.

The proposed '4D RoPE' is technically under-justified. Its spatial coordinates are dataset-wide mean joint locations rather than the actual time-varying 3D coordinates of each motion, so it primarily encodes canonical joint identity, not dynamic 3D position. Moreover, queries use a three-way RoPE partition while keys use a four-way partition; the paper does not explain how the channel rotations are aligned so that the usual relative-position interpretation of RoPE remains valid.

Several claimed capabilities exceed the evidence. Training explicitly retains only single-person clips, and the appendix concedes that different poses for multiple people are unsupported, yet the paper repeatedly advertises multi-character open-world animation. Generalization to unusual anatomy is likewise contradicted by the documented failure case.

The ablation does not isolate motion attention itself, compare it with ordinary cross-attention, or test the reference-conditioning design. Tokenizer reconstruction is presented only qualitatively, without MPJPE, velocity/acceleration error, codebook perplexity, or comparison to simpler motion encoders.

The codebook analysis is insufficiently defined and appears internally inconsistent: if 'usage frequency' denotes the fraction of token assignments, 2.9% of 8,192 codes cannot each have frequency above 15%. The normalization underlying the reported thresholds must be specified before these results are interpretable.

Reproducibility and data governance are limited by the undisclosed mixture of public, web-crawled, and AI-generated training videos. Exact sources, licenses, deduplication, benchmark-overlap checks, and consent procedures are absent, leaving both contamination and copyright concerns unresolved.

Using raw SMPL joint sequences rather than rendered pose images is a sensible direction that could reduce dependence on pixel-level alignment.
The reported TikTok results are promising for FVD, FID-VID, LPIPS, and FID, and the paper includes several architectural ablations and extensive qualitative examples.
The authors provide useful implementation details, training costs, failure cases, and a discussion of misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not established. There is no controlled comparison against a 2D-rendered-pose model using the same CogVideoX backbone, training data, parameter budget, and optimization. Comparisons between substantially different systems cannot show that motion tokenization itself causes the reported gains.

The evaluation is too narrow for the broad open-world claims. Quantitative testing uses only TikTok sequences 335-340, while generalization to unseen styles, anatomy, motions, and multiple characters is supported primarily by selected images rather than additional datasets, systematic sampling, or human evaluation.

The metrics do not adequately test the main claims. There is no direct motion-adherence metric, pose error, identity-similarity measure, temporal-consistency analysis, or evaluation of robustness to reference-driving misalignment. FID-style metrics alone cannot substantiate accurate motion transfer, identity preservation, or disentanglement.

The paper incorrectly states that the method is superior across all metrics: Table 1 shows worse PSNR than UniAnimate and Human-DiT and worse SSIM than Champ, UniAnimate, and Human-DiT. The FVD improvement over Animate Anyone 2 is also modest, despite the prominently advertised 65% improvement on FID-VID.

Baseline comparability is uncertain because Table 1 mixes newly evaluated systems with numbers copied from original papers. The proposed method additionally uses a 5B foundation model, approximately 7B trainable parameters, and a separately curated dataset, without compute-, data-, or backbone-matched baselines, confidence intervals, or significance analysis.

The technical novelty is overstated. The so-called 4D tokenizer is essentially a conventional VQ-VAE applying 2D convolutions over time and joint axes to sequences of 3D joints. Moreover, the spatial RoPE coordinates come from dataset-wide mean joint positions rather than the actual time-varying coordinates, so the advertised 4D positional encoding mainly supplies time and canonical joint identity rather than genuine per-token 4D location.

The ablations are incomplete: there is no removal of motion attention itself, no controlled rendered-pose alternative, no comparison with established motion tokenizers, and no numerical reconstruction or motion-quality evaluation of 4DMoT. The appendix's qualitative skeleton reconstruction and code-usage plots are insufficient validation.

The claimed multiple-character capability is misleadingly broad. The appendix explicitly says the system cannot animate multiple people with different poses, because its training pipeline retains only single-person clips. This important restriction conflicts with the headline open-world presentation.

Reproducibility and data governance are weak. The 5K-clip training set combines vaguely specified public, web-crawled, and AI-generated sources but is not documented sufficiently for reconstruction or licensing review. Copyright and consent risks are acknowledged, yet the proposed safeguards are only future plans.

Overall, the approach is plausible and the visual results are encouraging, but the unsupported attribution of gains, limited and potentially incomparable evaluation, overstated claims, and weak reproducibility keep the work below the acceptance threshold for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful alternative to rendered 2D pose conditioning: discretizing SMPL joint sequences and conditioning a video DiT through dedicated motion cross-attention.
The combination of a motion VQ-VAE, motion-aware attention, four-axis positional encoding, and classifier-free guidance is technically coherent and well motivated.
Results on the TikTok benchmark are strong, especially the substantial FID-VID improvement (6.98 versus 20.64 for the next reported result), alongside competitive FVD, FID, and LPIPS.

The ablations cover quantization, several positional-encoding variants, and guidance scale. They consistently support the selected design, with particularly large degradation when the proposed positional encoding is replaced.
Qualitative results span photorealistic, animated, stylized, full-body, half-body, and unusual-reference settings, suggesting useful generalization beyond conventional human-animation examples.

The architecture, optimization settings, computational cost, dataset filtering process, limitations, and misuse risks are described in reasonable detail. Failure cases involving unusual anatomy and hands are explicitly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central claim that raw motion tokens are superior to 2D-rendered pose conditions is not isolated experimentally. A controlled baseline using the same CogVideoX backbone, training data, compute, and conditioning architecture but 2D pose inputs is needed; comparisons against independently trained systems cannot establish that the representation itself causes the gain.

The quantitative evaluation is narrow: TikTok sequences 335–340 amount to only six test sequences. Open-world, cross-style, unusual-motion, and multi-character claims are supported mainly by selected qualitative examples, without a broader benchmark, user study, or motion/identity adherence measurements.

Table 1 is not fully controlled: some baselines are rerun while others are copied from their papers, and the manuscript does not establish identical preprocessing, frame counts, sampling, or metric implementations. Uncertainty across clips or random seeds is also absent.

The claim of superiority across all metrics is inaccurate: Human-DiT and UniAnimate report higher PSNR and SSIM. The FVD improvement over Animate Anyone 2 is also modest, even though FID-VID and FID improve substantially.

The proposed '4D RoPE' uses dataset-mean joint coordinates rather than the actual per-sequence 3D coordinates. It therefore appears to encode time and canonical joint identity/anatomy more directly than dynamic 4D position; the terminology and claimed invariances need sharper justification.

Multi-character framing is potentially misleading. The appendix states that the system cannot animate multiple people with different poses, so the demonstrated multi-character cases apparently apply one shared motion condition to all depicted characters.

Reproducibility is limited by the 7B-parameter model, substantial H100 training requirement, and a curated 5K-clip dataset that is not committed for release. The mixture of web-crawled and AI-generated data lacks detailed provenance, licensing, deduplication, and consent analysis.

No direct quantitative comparison is provided against closely related 3D-guided methods under matched conditions, nor are robustness tests reported for errors in SMPL estimation, camera motion, occlusion, or distribution shifts in body proportions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem and proposes a coherent end-to-end framework combining discrete 3D-joint motion tokenization with motion-conditioned video diffusion.
The method is implemented on two substantial video-generation backbones, suggesting reasonable architectural portability and scalability.
Reported results on TikTok and Fashion are strong across several reconstruction and distributional metrics, with particularly large FID/FVD improvements on TikTok.
The paper provides useful component ablations, extensive qualitative examples, and fairly detailed architecture and training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central claim that tokenized 4D motion is superior to rendered pose guidance is not established by a controlled comparison. There is no same-backbone, same-data, same-training-budget baseline conditioned on skeleton, depth, or SMPL renderings; comparisons against independently trained published systems confound representation, backbone scale, and training data.

The evaluation does not directly measure the claimed motion controllability. PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD primarily measure reconstruction or visual distributions; no 2D/3D pose error, motion-alignment metric, identity metric, or human preference study is reported.

The strongest claims—arbitrary-character animation, non-human transfer, and open-world zero-shot generalization—are supported only by selected qualitative frames. Static figures cannot establish temporal coherence, and no systematic out-of-domain benchmark or quantitative evaluation is provided.

The novelty and terminology are overstated. Quantizing 3D joint trajectories with a VQ-VAE and injecting them through cross-attention are closely related to established motion-token and conditional-generation techniques. Moreover, the proposed '4D RoPE' uses fixed dataset-mean joint locations rather than the actual time-varying 3D coordinates, so it primarily encodes time and joint identity rather than each token's true 4D position.

Subtracting the entire first-frame joint configuration discards absolute starting pose and orientation information, yet the paper does not analyze failure modes arising from this information loss or explain how motions with similar displacements but different absolute poses are distinguished.

Experimental reporting is insufficiently rigorous: most baseline values are copied from their respective papers rather than reproduced under a unified protocol; test-set sample counts, uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, inference cost, and statistical significance are absent. The tokenizer is also called compact despite using 3072-dimensional codes, without rate, memory, or computational comparisons.

Reproducibility and data governance remain problematic. Training relies on a curated web-crawled dataset whose sources, licenses, consent conditions, and release status are unspecified. The ethics discussion acknowledges copyright and impersonation risks but only proposes future safeguards despite stating that a commercial deployment already exists.

strengths: The paper explores a relevant problem and presents a coherent end-to-end system combining motion tokenization with motion-conditioned video diffusion.
Results on TikTok and Fashion are numerically strong across several standard reconstruction and distributional metrics, and the paper includes experiments at two model scales.
The ablations cover quantization, differential coordinates, positional encodings, and classifier-free guidance; the appendix also provides useful architectural and optimization details.
The qualitative examples suggest potentially useful generalization across character styles and subject categories.
weaknesses: The central claim that motion tokens are superior to 2D-rendered pose conditioning is not established by a controlled comparison. There is no matched-backbone, matched-data baseline that replaces the proposed tokens with skeleton, depth, or mesh renderings. Consequently, gains may arise from the much larger backbones, training data, or optimization rather than the claimed representation.

The evaluation does not directly measure the main claimed benefit: motion controllability. No pose accuracy, joint error, motion-alignment metric, temporal consistency study, or human evaluation is reported. PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD cannot substantiate claims such as precise motion transfer or physically plausible motion.

The open-world and non-human generalization claims rely on selected static frames. There is no quantitative out-of-distribution benchmark, systematic failure analysis, baseline evaluation on these cases, or video-level user study. Static images are especially insufficient for assessing animation quality and temporal artifacts.

Comparisons are difficult to interpret: most baseline numbers are copied from their papers, model capacity varies drastically, and MTVCraft uses an unspecified proprietary mixture of public and web-crawled data. The substantial 6B-to-18B improvement is not disentangled from the stronger Wan backbone, while no parameter-, data-, or compute-matched comparison is provided.

The terminology overstates the technical novelty. The input is not raw 4D motion but estimated SMPL-derived 3D joints over time, a standard motion representation. The proposed 4D RoPE uses dataset-mean joint locations rather than sample-specific 3D coordinates, so much of its spatial component functions as a fixed joint-identity encoding. Moreover, vision pixel coordinates and SMPL-space coordinates are not shown to share a meaningful geometric scale, weakening the claimed physical alignment.

The tokenizer itself is inadequately validated. Reconstruction is shown only qualitatively, without MPJPE, acceleration, velocity, foot-contact, or comparison against established motion tokenizers. The codebook analysis is also unclear: labeling 66.8% of 8192 entries as having 1%-15% usage is mathematically inconsistent if these are ordinary normalized per-code frequencies, suggesting either an erroneous definition or insufficient reporting.

Several ablations remain ambiguous or incomplete. The meaning of '3D quantization' is not rigorously specified; failed alternatives are assessed after only 10K steps; and there is no isolation of motion attention from ordinary cross-attention, canonical joint embeddings, or continuous-coordinate conditioning of comparable capacity.

Evaluation sample counts, resolutions, preprocessing details, checkpoint-selection procedures, repeated-run variance, and confidence intervals are absent. FID/FVD are highly sensitive to these choices, so the reported margins are not independently assessable.

Reproducibility is limited despite the paper's claim: the 30K training set is not identified or released, web sources and licenses are unspecified, filtering is only partially documented, and reproducing the 6B/18B training requires substantial resources. The generic ethics statement does not adequately address consent, copyright, demographic bias, deepfake misuse, or the asserted commercial deployment.

Overall, the idea is plausible and the reported results are promising, but the paper does not provide sufficiently controlled or direct evidence for its principal scientific claims. These are substantive evaluation and attribution problems rather than minor omissions, placing it below the top-tier acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and meaningful contribution: replacing rendered 2D pose conditions with discrete tokens derived from temporally varying 3D joints is a promising direction for character animation.

The proposed system is technically coherent, combining a motion VQ-VAE, motion-to-vision cross-attention, positional encoding, and motion-aware classifier-free guidance within modern video diffusion transformers.
Results on both TikTok and Fashion are strong across image-quality and video-quality metrics. The 6B model is already competitive, while the 18B model produces further consistent gains.
Ablations cover quantization, differential coordinates, depth, positional-encoding variants, and guidance scale on two datasets. They provide useful evidence for several design choices.
The qualitative results are broad and visually compelling, particularly for stylized characters, non-human subjects, difficult motions, and pose/reference misalignment.

The architecture is demonstrated on two substantially different backbones, suggesting that the conditioning mechanism is reasonably portable. Implementation and training details are also comparatively thorough.
weaknesses: The central claim that tokenized 4D motion is superior to rendered pose conditioning lacks the most important controlled experiment: the same backbone, data, optimization, and parameter budget using tokens versus skeleton, mesh, or depth renderings. Comparisons with independently trained prior systems cannot isolate the representation's contribution.

The 18B result is confounded by a much stronger pretrained backbone, retained text conditioning, and a different fine-tuning strategy. Consequently, it does not by itself establish a scaling property of the proposed method.

The paper evaluates pose control mostly through reconstruction-oriented metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, FID, and FVD. It lacks direct motion-control measurements, including 2D/3D keypoint error, temporal acceleration or jitter, identity similarity, and a human preference study. This weakens claims of precise motion transfer and unparalleled generalization.

The so-called 4D RoPE uses dataset-averaged, static joint locations rather than the dynamic 3D coordinates of each motion token. It therefore largely encodes time and canonical joint identity. The paper should moderate its geometric interpretation and explain coordinate normalization and scale compatibility with vision-token coordinates.

Baseline values are mostly copied from the respective papers, while only selected missing metrics are re-evaluated. Differences in preprocessing, frame selection, resolution, and evaluation implementations may compromise comparability; uncertainty estimates and repeated-run variation are also absent.

Several highly relevant recent systems discussed in related work, including HumanDiT, HyperMotion, DreamActor, and Wan-Animate, are not evaluated. Open-world evidence is almost entirely qualitative and consists of selected examples.

Reproducibility remains limited by the unreleased or insufficiently specified 30K-clip training corpus and the substantial compute requirement. The manuscript says code is released, but the anonymized PDF does not provide a verifiable artifact.

The use of web-crawled human videos, together with claimed commercial deployment, raises consent, privacy, copyright, and deepfake concerns. The ethics section acknowledges misuse only briefly and does not document data provenance, licensing, subject protections, or concrete safeguards.
